title: Design a URL shortener (and Pastebin)
scopeHtml: Scope: requirements, API, estimates, ID generation, redirect path, caching, analytics, Pastebin variant.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
A URL shortener turns a long link into a tiny one (sho.rt/aZ3k9Q) and, when someone opens the tiny link, sends them to the long one. That is the whole product. Bitly, TinyURL and Twitter's t.co do this. Pastebin is the same shape with text instead of a URL.

Functional requirements

  • Create a short link from a long URL (optionally a custom alias and an expiry).
  • Open a short link and get redirected to the long URL.
  • Optional: click analytics, delete or expire a link, per-user dashboard.

Non-functional requirements

  • Redirect latency under 50 ms p99 (it sits in the path of every click).
  • Availability 99.99% for redirects; creation can tolerate a bit less.
  • Links must not collide and should not be easily guessable or enumerable.
  • Read-heavy: about 100 reads for every 1 write.

Decision gravity. Choose 301 vs 302 now: a 301 (permanent) is cached by browsers forever, so you lose click analytics and can never change the target. A 302 (temporary) costs you a hit per click but keeps control. Bitly uses 301 for some cases and tracks clicks anyway through other means; if analytics matter, use 302. It is reversible only for new links, because browsers already cached old 301s.

Everyday analogy. A coat-check ticket: a tiny numbered tag stands for a big bulky coat stored in the back.

Common interview traps.

  • Starting to design before asking about analytics, expiry and custom aliases.
  • Using 301 and then being asked how you count clicks.
  • Not stating the read:write ratio.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
Two public endpoints plus a few management ones. Keep them REST and idempotent where possible.

POST /v1/links
Authorization: Bearer <api_key>
{ "longUrl": "https://example.com/a/very/long/path?x=1",
  "customAlias": "summer-sale",     // optional
  "expiresAt": "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z" }   // optional

201 Created
{ "shortCode": "aZ3k9Q",
  "shortUrl": "https://sho.rt/aZ3k9Q",
  "longUrl": "https://example.com/a/very/long/path?x=1",
  "expiresAt": "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z" }

409 Conflict   -> customAlias already taken
400 Bad Request -> invalid or blocked URL
429 Too Many Requests -> per-key limit hit
GET /aZ3k9Q
302 Found
Location: https://example.com/a/very/long/path?x=1
Cache-Control: private, max-age=0

404 Not Found -> unknown code
410 Gone      -> expired or deleted
GET    /v1/links/aZ3k9Q/stats?from=2026-11-01&to=2026-11-09
200 { "clicks": 12873, "byDay": [...], "topCountries": [...] }
DELETE /v1/links/aZ3k9Q        -> 204

Idempotency: creating the same long URL twice may return the same code (dedupe by hash) or a new one. Decide and say it. Bitly returns a new link per user; many designs dedupe per user only.

Industry example. Bitly's public API is exactly this: POST to create, GET on the short domain redirects, a separate stats endpoint.

Everyday analogy. A reception desk: one window to register a new tag, another window that reads a tag and points you to the room.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting analytics counters inside the redirect API response path synchronously.
  • Forgetting 404 vs 410 and error codes.
  • No auth or rate limit on the create endpoint (spam and phishing).

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 100M new links per month, 100:1 read:write.

Quantity Calculation Result
Write QPS 100M / (30 x 86,400 s = 2.6M s) about 40/s, peak 120/s
Read QPS 40 x 100 about 4,000/s, peak 12,000/s
Record size code 7 B + long URL ~200 B + metadata ~50 B ~300 B
Storage in 5 years 100M x 12 x 5 = 6B links x 300 B ~1.8 TB
Bandwidth out 4,000/s x ~500 B response ~2 MB/s (tiny)
Cache size (hot 20%) 20% of daily reads' unique links ~tens of GB, fits in one Redis

A bigger scale variant. The table above is a mid-size service. A public Bitly-class service is far more read-heavy: assume 100M daily users, about 1M new links a day (about 12 writes/s), about 1B redirects a day (about 12,000/s on average, 60,000/s at peak, a read:write ratio near 1,000:1) and about 1B stored links. State your own ratio out loud: it decides whether one primary plus cache is enough or whether you need a key-value store partitioned by code. Set separate availability targets: redirects 99.99% (a dead short link on a printed poster cannot be fixed) and creation 99.9%, so on the read side choose availability over consistency. Support an Idempotency-Key header on POST /urls so a retried create returns the same link instead of a second one.

Code length. Base62 (a-z, A-Z, 0-9). 62^6 = 56.8 billion, 62^7 = 3.5 trillion. 6B links in 5 years fits in 7 characters with a big safety margin; 6 characters would be close to the limit once collisions and waste are included. So use 7.

What this tells you. 12,000 reads/s is easy for a cache; 1.8 TB is easy for one sharded or even single big Postgres/Cassandra cluster. The hard part is ID generation without collisions and cache efficiency, not raw throughput.

Everyday analogy. Counting how many coat tickets you hand out per day before deciding how big the coat room is.

Common interview traps.

  • Computing QPS with 86,400 s/day but monthly numbers (units mismatch).
  • Choosing a 5-character code and not checking the keyspace.
  • Over-sharding a 2 TB dataset on day one.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components

  • Redirect service: stateless, looks up code in Redis, falls back to the DB, returns 302.
  • Create service: validates URL, gets a unique ID, base62-encodes it, stores (code, longUrl, userId, createdAt, expiresAt).
  • Link DB: key-value access by code. DynamoDB or Cassandra fit well (point lookups, easy sharding); Postgres also works at this size.
  • Click queue: a Kafka topic; the redirect fires and forgets an event so latency is unaffected.

Decision gravity. Choose a key-value style store keyed by shortCode. Alternatives: relational with an index. It breaks if you later need rich queries ("all links of user X sorted by date") on the same store; solve with a secondary index or a second table. Moving store is a one-way door only in effort (data migration), not in correctness, because the access pattern is just get/put by key.

Industry examples. Bitly's published engineering posts describe sharded MySQL with caching; many modern clones use DynamoDB or Cassandra.

Everyday analogy. A front desk (redirect) with a fast pigeonhole shelf (cache) in front of the big archive room (DB).

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing an SQL join-heavy schema for what is a key-value lookup.
  • Putting analytics writes in the redirect transaction.
  • No cache in front of the DB for a 100:1 read workload.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
ID generation and collisions

How do we get a unique 7-char code? Three options:

  1. Hash the long URL (MD5/SHA-256, take the first 41 bits, since 62^7 is about 2^41.7, and base62). Simple, same URL gives same code, but collisions happen (birthday paradox: with 6B items and 3.5T keyspace, collisions are frequent). You must check the DB and retry with a salt. Extra read per write.
  2. Counter + base62. A global auto-increment ID (for example from a ticket server or a range allocator) encoded in base62. No collisions by construction. Downside: codes are sequential and guessable, and a single counter is a bottleneck/SPOF.
  3. Pre-generated key service (KGS). A background job fills a table of random unused 7-char keys; app servers each pull a batch of, say, 1,000 keys into memory. No collision, no coordination per request, not guessable. If a server dies you lose at most its batch (acceptable waste).

Chosen: range allocator (each server leases 10,000 IDs from a counter in ZooKeeper/DB) then scramble the number with a reversible shuffle (a Feistel permutation or multiply by a large odd prime mod 62^7) before base62, so codes are not sequential. Reversible and cheap.

Safety net: an atomic conditional insert. Even with unique ids, never "check if the code exists, then insert": two writers can both see "free". Write with a conditional put (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, DynamoDB attribute_not_exists(code), Cassandra IF NOT EXISTS) and treat a conflict as "retry with a new code". This also protects custom aliases, which share the same key space as generated codes, and survives losing the counter (a restored range may re-issue ids). For a multi-region setup, give each region its own slice of the id space (for example the top bits of the id) so regions never hand out the same range.

# Reversible scramble so sequential ids look random
M = 62**7
K = 2654435761          # odd, coprime with M
def scramble(n):  return (n * K) % M

Decision gravity. The ID scheme is a one-way door: once codes are public they live forever; changing the scheme later means supporting both. When it breaks: the allocator being down stops creates (reads still work), so run it replicated or let servers keep a buffer.

Redirect path and caching

Read path: LB, redirect service, Redis GET code. On miss, read DB and set Redis with TTL 24h. With a Zipf-like distribution (a few viral links get most clicks), an 80/20 cache hit rate of 90%+ is typical, taking DB load from 12,000/s to under 1,200/s.

  • Redis config: maxmemory 32gb, maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru, 2 replicas.
  • Negative caching: cache 404s for 60 s to survive scans of random codes.
  • Hot key: a viral link could hit one Redis shard hard; add a tiny in-process cache (1 s TTL) on redirect servers.

Production incident pattern. Symptom: p99 latency jumps and DB CPU spikes after a celebrity tweet. Metric: cache hit ratio drops or one Redis shard's CPU is pinned. Fix: local cache + request coalescing (single flight) so 1,000 simultaneous misses cause one DB read.

Analytics without slowing redirects

On every redirect, publish {code, ts, ip, userAgent, referrer} to Kafka asynchronously (fire and forget, batched, acks=1). Workers aggregate per code per minute and write to ClickHouse/Druid or a counters table. If Kafka is down, drop events rather than fail the redirect: clicks are best effort, redirects are the product.

Expiry and cleanup

Store expiresAt. On read, check it and return 410. A nightly job deletes expired rows (or use DynamoDB TTL / Cassandra TTL). Do not recycle codes immediately; keep a tombstone window so an old shared link does not suddenly point to a stranger's page.

Abuse and security

Scan long URLs against Safe Browsing lists on creation and again periodically. Rate limit creates per API key and per IP. Do not allow javascript: or internal IP targets (SSRF/open-redirect abuse).

Pastebin variant

Same system, but the value is a text blob (up to 10 MB) instead of a URL. Differences:

  • Store content in object storage (S3) keyed by id, metadata (id, owner, expiry, visibility) in the DB.
  • Size: 1M pastes/day x 10 KB average = 10 GB/day, 3.6 TB/year; dominated by blobs, so put S3 plus a CDN in front.
  • Add a content hash to dedupe identical pastes.
  • Support expiry options (10 min, 1 day, never) and private links (unguessable ID, longer, random).

Industry example. GitHub Gists and Pastebin.com keep text in object/file storage with metadata in a database.

Everyday analogy. The key service is a drawer of pre-printed unique tickets that each cashier takes a stack of, so nobody ever hands out the same number twice.

Common interview traps.

  • Hashing and ignoring collision handling.
  • Sequential counter codes that expose how many links you have and are scrapeable.
  • Letting analytics failures break redirects.
  • Storing paste bodies in the database instead of blob storage.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Clarifying questions first: custom alias, expiry, analytics, scale.
  • Numbers: QPS, storage, and why 7 base62 characters.
  • A clear ID strategy with its trade-offs (hash vs counter vs key service) and collision handling.
  • Read-optimised design: cache aside, hit ratio reasoning, hot keys.
  • 301 vs 302 and what it implies for analytics.
  • Failure thinking: what if the ID service, Redis or Kafka is down; what degrades and what does not.
  • Seniors also mention abuse, GDPR deletion, multi-region reads, and the cost of each choice, and know which choices are reversible.

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping into sharding when the dataset is 2 TB.
  • Not discussing security and abuse.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Tiny links are a key-value lookup: code -> longUrl; reads dominate 100:1, about 12k/s peak.
  • 7 base62 characters give 3.5 trillion codes; plenty for 6B links in 5 years.
  • Pick the ID strategy deliberately: range allocator plus reversible scramble avoids collisions and guessability; it is the one-way door.
  • Serve redirects from Redis (cache aside, negative caching, local cache for hot keys), DB as the source of truth.
  • Use 302 if you need click analytics; send click events asynchronously through Kafka and never let them block the redirect.
  • Pastebin = same design, but blob in S3, metadata in the DB, CDN in front.

questions.promptHtml: In a URL shortener, should the redirect return 301 or 302? What does each cost you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is a small decision with a big product consequence. It shows whether you think about analytics, caching and reversibility before drawing boxes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I use 302 if we care about click analytics or may change the target. A 301 is permanent, so browsers and proxies cache it and never ask us again: no click counts, and we can never repoint the link for users who already visited. A 302 costs one request per click, which our redirect service is built to handle anyway.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• 301 Moved Permanently: the browser may cache the mapping indefinitely. Later clicks from the same browser never reach our servers.
  • 302 Found (temporary): the browser asks us every time, so every click is observable and the target is editable, expirable and deletable.
  • Our load is about 100 reads per write, but a cache-backed redirect at 12k/s is cheap, so the extra hits from 302 are not a cost problem.
  • It is a one-way door for old links: once a 301 is cached in browsers you cannot recall it. It is reversible only for new links.
GET /aZ3k9Q  -> 302 Found
Location: https://example.com/long/path
Cache-Control: private, max-age=0

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Picking 301 "because it is faster" and then being asked how you count clicks.
  • Forgetting 404 (unknown) vs 410 (expired or deleted).
  • Setting a long Cache-Control on a 302 and accidentally getting the 301 behaviour.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can we ever use 301? -> Yes for links that are guaranteed permanent and where analytics are not needed; it saves load and gives SEO link juice to the target.
  2. How do you expire a link already cached by a browser? -> With 302 plus max-age=0 you do not have that problem; with 301 you cannot.
  3. How do you count clicks if some clients ignore cache headers? -> Count server-side at the redirect, asynchronously via a queue; treat counts as approximate.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "301 is permanent, 302 is temporary". The senior answer ties the choice to analytics, editability and the one-way nature of cached 301s, and says it is reversible only for new links.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team shipped 301s, later added a paid analytics tier, and found a large share of clicks never reached their servers.

questions.promptHtml: Compare hashing the long URL, a counter with base62, and a pre-generated key service for creating short codes. Which would you pick and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: ID generation is the real hard part of this problem. They want to see collision handling, guessability and failure thinking, not just "base62".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Hashing is simple but collides and needs a check-and-retry. A plain counter never collides but codes are sequential, scrapeable, and the counter is a bottleneck. I would use a range allocator: each app server leases a block of, say, 10,000 ids, then I scramble each number with a reversible permutation and base62 it, and I still use a conditional insert as a safety net.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Keyspace: 62^7 is about 3.5 trillion, enough for 6B links in 5 years with big margin; 62^6 (56.8B) is too tight once waste is counted.

Option Collisions Guessable Coordination
Hash (first 41 bits of MD5/SHA) Yes (birthday), need retry with salt No Extra read per write
Counter + base62 None Yes, sequential Single counter is a SPOF
Key service (pre-generated random keys) None No Batches per server, small waste
Range allocator + scramble None No One lease per 10k ids

The scramble is multiply by an odd constant coprime with 62^7, mod 62^7: reversible, cheap, makes sequential ids look random. The conditional insert (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, or DynamoDB attribute_not_exists) protects custom aliases, which share the key space, and survives a restored counter re-issuing ids.

M = 62**7
K = 2654435761   # odd, coprime with M
def scramble(n): return (n * K) % M

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Check-then-insert in two steps: two writers both see "free".
  • Using a 5 or 6 character code without computing the keyspace.
  • Forgetting that custom aliases live in the same namespace as generated codes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the allocator is down? -> Servers keep a buffered range, so creates continue for a while; reads are unaffected; run the allocator replicated.
  2. Multi-region? -> Give each region its own slice of the id space (top bits) so ranges never overlap.
  3. Can you change the scheme later? -> It is a one-way door: public codes live forever, so you would have to support both schemes at lookup.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "base62 of a hash". The senior compares three schemes, names the guessability and SPOF costs, adds the atomic conditional insert, and calls out that the choice cannot be undone.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A sequential-code shortener leaked its total link count and got fully scraped, exposing private document links.

questions.contextHtml: Your shortener serves 100M new links a month and 100:1 reads, running on one Postgres primary plus Redis. Product now says the campaign business will push it to a Bitly-class service: 1M new links a day, 1B redirects a day, 1B stored links, peak 5x average. The interviewer gives you five minutes and a whiteboard.
questions.promptHtml: Do the capacity math for the new scale and say what, if anything, must change in the architecture.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Multiplies everything by 10 without showing arithmetic, jumps to "shard everything", and never states the read:write ratio or availability targets.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 1B redirects a day average or peak? Do we keep click analytics (changes the write path)? Are creates and redirects in the same SLO? Is multi-region required?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I start with the numbers.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Reads are the bottleneck, not storage; the ID service is no problem at 12 writes/s.
  4. How I'd verify each: Math. Writes: 1M / 86,400 = about 12/s. Reads: 1B / 86,400 = about 11,600/s average, 5x = about 58,000/s peak, ratio about 1,000:1. Storage: 1B x 300 B = 300 GB. Cache: with a Zipf distribution, top 20% of daily unique links is tens of GB, fits in a small Redis cluster. Bandwidth: 58k x 500 B = about 29 MB/s.
  5. Root cause: None; the design question is whether one primary and one cache still suffice.
  6. Fix: 300 GB fits one Postgres, but 58k/s with a 90% hit rate leaves 5.8k/s on the DB: still fine. I would still move the store to a key-value system partitioned by code (DynamoDB or Cassandra) for availability, run Redis with replicas, add a 1 s in-process cache for viral keys, and split SLOs: redirects 99.99%, create 99.9%, preferring availability over consistency on reads.
  7. Prevention: Dashboards for cache hit ratio, DB QPS, p99 redirect latency; load test at 2x peak.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not shard on day one for storage reasons; 300 GB does not need it. I would not make redirects wait on analytics.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Write rate becomes 1,000/s? -> Range allocator still fine; the DB write path moves to a partitioned store.
  • Cache hit ratio is only 60%? -> Re-check TTL and eviction, add negative caching; the DB must then handle 23k/s, which means partitioning.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team sharded a 2 TB store at launch and spent a year operating shards; the actual pain was a single viral link overloading one cache node.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: arithmetic missing or off by 10x; shards by reflex.
  • Hire: correct QPS, storage and cache math; identifies read path as the focus.
  • Strong hire: also splits SLOs, handles hot keys and states what is deliberately not scaled.

questions.contextHtml: The interviewer says only: "Design a URL shortener." No numbers, no other requirements. You have 40 minutes.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do in the first five minutes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Starts drawing a load balancer and a database immediately, or recites a memorised design without asking anything.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Functional: custom aliases? expiry? delete? per-user dashboard? analytics (this decides 301 vs 302)? Non-functional: write volume per month, read:write ratio, redirect latency target, availability target, global or one region? Abuse: are anonymous creates allowed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: I write the agreed scope on the board in two lists: in scope, out of scope. Anything unanswered I state as an assumption: 100M links/month, 100:1 reads, p99 under 50 ms.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The real difficulty will be ID generation and cache efficiency, not raw throughput.
  4. How I'd verify each: Quick estimates: about 40 writes/s, 4,000 reads/s, 1.8 TB over 5 years; 7 base62 characters.
  5. Root cause: Not applicable; this is requirement discovery.
  6. Fix: I propose the flow: two paths (create, redirect), then ask which part they want deep.
  7. Prevention: Re-check the assumptions at the end against the design.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I do not ask twenty questions; I ask the five that change the design and assume the rest aloud.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Assume anything you like" -> State your assumptions and note which ones you would confirm first.
  • "Analytics yes, but best effort" -> 302 plus async event queue; clicks may be dropped, redirects must not fail.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A design started without asking about analytics, chose 301, and was rewritten when marketing asked for click counts after launch.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no questions; starts with components.
  • Hire: asks about alias, expiry, analytics and scale; states assumptions.
  • Strong hire: ties each question to a design consequence and keeps scope bounded.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate wrote custom-alias creation. Under load tests two users occasionally both get a 201 for summer-sale, and one of them later sees the other's link.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
public Link create(String alias, String longUrl) {
    if (repo.exists(alias)) {
        throw new Conflict("alias taken");
    }
    Link link = new Link(alias, longUrl);
    repo.save(link);          // plain upsert by primary key
    return link;
}
fun create(alias: String, longUrl: String): Link {
    if (repo.exists(alias)) throw Conflict("alias taken")
    val link = Link(alias, longUrl)
    repo.save(link)           // plain upsert by primary key
    return link
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain how it shows up, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Says "add a lock" or "synchronize the method", which does nothing across several app servers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which store? Does save upsert or insert? Are custom aliases and generated codes in the same key space?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Nothing is exposed yet, but I would find affected aliases by scanning for overwritten rows (compare createdAt and owner changes in audit logs).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Check-then-act race (two servers both see "free"), plus an upsert that overwrites silently.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run two concurrent creates of the same alias against the store in a test; look at the DB log for two writes to the same key.
  5. Root cause: exists then save is not atomic. Both requests pass the check, the second save overwrites the first. A JVM lock cannot help because the race is across servers.
  6. Fix: Make the store enforce uniqueness in one operation: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (check the affected row count), DynamoDB attribute_not_exists(code), or Cassandra IF NOT EXISTS. On conflict return 409 for custom aliases, or retry with a new code for generated ones.
  7. Prevention: A concurrency test that fires 50 parallel creates of one alias and asserts exactly one 201; review rule: never "check then insert".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a distributed lock for this; the database already provides atomic conditional writes and it is simpler and cheaper.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cassandra IF NOT EXISTS cost? -> It uses Paxos (lightweight transaction), slower; fine at 12 creates/s.
  • Alias reuse after delete? -> Keep a tombstone window so old shared links never point to a stranger.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A vanity-link feature silently overwrote a partner's alias during a launch; the fix was one conditional insert and an alert on 409 rates.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests synchronized.
  • Hire: names the race and uses a conditional insert.
  • Strong hire: also covers shared key space, retry for generated codes and a concurrency test.

questions.subtopic: Cache stampede on a viral link
questions.contextHtml:
A celebrity tweets a short link at 14:02. Within a minute: redirect p99 goes from 12 ms to 2.4 s, DB CPU 95%, and one Redis shard is pinned.

14:01  redis shard-2 cpu 38%   db qps 900    hit ratio 93%
14:03  redis shard-2 cpu 100%  db qps 11,400 hit ratio 71%
14:03  redirect-svc timeouts: 4,200/s   Kafka producer errors: 0

Link aZ3k9Q is getting about 40,000 clicks/s. The cache TTL on it was 60 s and it just expired. Someone suggests "add more DB replicas".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Scales the DB or restarts Redis; never connects the spike to one key and the TTL expiry.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the load on a single key? Did the TTL expire at 14:02? Are there other hot keys? Is the key distribution in Redis even?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Manually set the hot key with a long TTL (for example 1 hour) so it stops missing; shed load on random-code misses; do not restart Redis.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) hot key on one shard plus stampede on expiry; (b) cache eviction pressure; (c) DB slow query. The DB qps rise says misses, and one pinned shard says one key.
  4. How I'd verify each: redis-cli --hotkeys or MONITOR sample, per-key hit counters, DB slow log (a primary-key lookup is not slow, it is simply too many).
  5. Root cause: One key gets 40k/s. When it expires, thousands of requests miss simultaneously and all hit the DB; and even when cached, a single key lives on a single Redis shard, which saturates.
  6. Fix: Short term: pin and extend the TTL. Long term: a 1 s in-process cache per redirect server (removes most Redis load for hot keys), request coalescing (single flight) so concurrent misses cause one DB read, and jittered TTLs.
  7. Prevention: Alert on per-shard CPU skew and hit ratio; load test with a Zipf distribution; hot key detection that auto-promotes keys to the local cache.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not scale the DB: the problem is 40k/s on one key. The local cache means a changed target may be stale for 1 s, acceptable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Link is deleted for abuse during the spike? -> Local cache TTL bounds staleness; push an invalidation for the key.
  • 100 redirect servers, each misses once per second? -> 100 DB reads/s for the key, trivial.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fixed 60 s TTL aligned across thousands of keys made the cache miss in waves every minute until jitter was added.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales DB or restarts Redis.
  • Hire: identifies hot key and stampede, adds local cache and coalescing.
  • Strong hire: adds jitter, per-shard skew alerting and explains the staleness trade-off.

questions.contextHtml: Click analytics are written synchronously into the Link DB in the same transaction as the redirect lookup (UPDATE links SET clicks = clicks + 1). Last week the analytics Kafka cluster was replaced; this week redirect error rate hit 8% during a broker maintenance because an intermediate "events" call was added in the request path. Marketing insists they cannot lose clicks.
questions.promptHtml: Redesign the click path. What do you tell marketing about accuracy?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Keeps analytics synchronous "to be correct", or says "just use exactly once" without cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How accurate must counts be (billing or dashboards)? Real-time or hourly? Who consumes them? Is a 0.1% loss acceptable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make the event publish fire-and-forget with a short timeout; on failure drop or buffer to local disk, so redirects never fail.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The synchronous call is the single cause; the row-level counter update also creates a hot row for viral links.
  4. How I'd verify each: Look at redirect error codes during maintenance; check lock waits on the hot row in the DB.
  5. Root cause: Best-effort data was put in the critical path of the product's main function.
  6. Fix: Redirect publishes {code, ts, ip, ua, referrer} to Kafka asynchronously (batched, acks=1). Workers aggregate per code per minute into ClickHouse/Druid or a counters table. If Kafka is down, drop events (or spill to a local buffer) rather than fail the redirect.
  7. Prevention: Metric for dropped events; reconciliation of sampled raw logs against aggregates; a chaos test that kills Kafka and checks redirect success.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: For billing-grade counts I would use a separate path (access logs shipped reliably, deduped by request id) instead of putting the guarantee on the redirect. I would not promise exact counts for a free dashboard.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Duplicates from consumer retries? -> At-least-once plus dedupe by event id, or accept small overcount.
  • Bots inflate clicks? -> Filter by user agent and rate at the aggregation stage; keep raw events.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "clicks" counter incremented in the primary DB became the hottest row in the system and caused lock waits during a campaign.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: synchronous writes.
  • Hire: async queue, drop on failure, separate aggregation.
  • Strong hire: distinguishes best-effort vs billing-grade, hot row problem and reconciliation.

questions.contextHtml: Your Pastebin stores paste bodies (average 10 KB, up to 10 MB) in a Postgres bytea column. 1M pastes/day: 10 GB/day, table now 4 TB, vacuum takes hours, backups take 18 hours, p99 reads are 400 ms. Reads are 50:1. You must move bodies to object storage with zero downtime and no lost pastes.
questions.promptHtml: Describe the target design and the migration plan.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Dump and restore overnight", or a big-bang cutover with no rollback.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are private pastes served through signed URLs? Retention and delete requirements (GDPR)? Is a few ms extra latency acceptable on first read? Is dedupe wanted?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Put a CDN in front of paste reads now; it cuts DB reads immediately.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Large blobs bloat the table, hurt vacuum, cache hit rate and backups.
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_total_relation_size, TOAST size, buffer cache hit ratio, pg_stat_user_tables for vacuum duration.
  5. Root cause: Blob content sits in the transactional store, which should hold only metadata.
  6. Fix: Target: metadata table (id, owner, expiry, visibility, contentHash, s3Key) in Postgres, bodies in S3 keyed by id (or hash for dedupe), CDN in front. Migration: (1) dual-write new pastes to S3 and DB; (2) background job copies old bodies to S3, verifies checksum, sets s3Key; (3) read path prefers S3, falls back to DB; (4) when 100% verified, stop DB reads, keep DB bodies a week, then null them and vacuum/repack.
  7. Prevention: A metric of "pastes without s3Key"; a periodic checksum audit; size limits at the API.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not delete DB bodies until the audit passes. Content-hash dedupe saves storage but complicates deletion (reference counting), so I would decide that explicitly.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Private pastes on a CDN? -> Unguessable long id, signed URLs with short expiry, Cache-Control: private.
  • Expired pastes? -> S3 lifecycle rules plus metadata TTL; keep tombstones so ids are not reused immediately.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A big-bang blob migration lost a few thousand pastes because the copy job ran while writes were still landing in the old path; dual-write fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: offline dump and restore.
  • Hire: object storage plus metadata, phased migration with fallback.
  • Strong hire: checksums, dual-write, rollback, dedupe/GDPR trade-off and private link handling.
